questions.question: What role did the Indian People’s Theatre Association (IPTA) play during the British rule?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Expressed dissent through art**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• The Indian People's Theatre Association (IPTA) was established in 1943 with the aim of using art as a tool for social and political change.
 
• It was actively involved in portraying the struggles against British colonial rule through performances, plays, and music.
 
• IPTA brought together artists, writers, and performers to advocate for freedom and social justice using creative mediums such as theatre and folk art.
 
• Its productions often highlighted social issues, including poverty, oppression, and exploitation by colonial powers.
 
• The association played a crucial role in fostering cultural nationalism and expressing dissent against British policies during India's independence movement.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Indian People's Theatre Association (IPTA):**

 
 
• IPTA was closely associated with the Progressive Writers' Association, which also aimed to use literature for societal change.
 
• The association played a key role in introducing realism in Indian theatre, focusing on the lives of marginalized communities.
 
• IPTA's work was inspired by global movements such as the Russian Revolution and anti-fascist struggles, blending these influences into Indian art.
 
• Prominent members included Balraj Sahni, Prithviraj Kapoor, and Salil Chowdhury, who contributed significantly to the cultural renaissance in India.
 
 
 
• **Art as a form of protest:**
 
 
• Art has historically been a powerful medium to challenge authority and inspire social change.
 
• During colonial rule, various forms of art—including paintings, music, and theatre—were used to promote nationalist sentiments.
 
• Folk traditions such as Bhakti poetry and local storytelling were adapted to criticize British policies and evoke patriotism.
 
 
 
• **Cultural Nationalism:**
 
 
• Cultural nationalism refers to the promotion of national identity through cultural expressions such as art, literature, and traditions.
 
• In colonial India, cultural nationalism played a significant role in unifying diverse communities against British rule.
 
 
 
• **Legacy of IPTA:**
 
 
• IPTA's influence extended into post-independence India, shaping progressive art and cinema.
 
• Its emphasis on social realism continues to inspire modern theatre and film movements in India.

questions.question: Who among the following was/were NOT part of the Santhal Rebellion?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Tana Bhagats**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• The **Santhal Rebellion (1855-56)** was led by tribal leaders **Sidhu, Kanho, Chand, and Bhairav Murmu** to resist British colonial oppression and exploitation by landlords and moneylenders.
 
• The rebellion primarily took place in the **Rajmahal Hills** of present-day Jharkhand, where the Santhal tribes united against oppressive policies.
 
• Tana Bhagats, a tribal group from the Oraon community, were not part of the Santhal Rebellion. They emerged later in 1914, as followers of Mahatma Gandhi's non-violent principles.
 
• The Santhal Rebellion was one of the significant tribal uprisings against British rule, marked by violent resistance to reclaim tribal autonomy and land rights.
 
• The rebellion was ultimately crushed by the British forces, but it led to the creation of the Santhal Pargana district in 1856 to address tribal grievances.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Santhal Rebellion (1855-56):**

 
 
• Also known as the Hul Rebellion, it was a tribal uprising led by the Santhal community against British rule and exploitation by zamindars and moneylenders.
 
• The rebellion marked a significant resistance movement before the Indian Revolt of 1857.
 
 
 
• **Tana Bhagats Movement (1914):**
 
 
• Founded by Jatra Oraon, the Tana Bhagats were a tribal reformist group inspired by Gandhian ideals of non-violence and self-purification.
 
• They opposed British taxes and participated in the Civil Disobedience Movement.
 
 
 
• **Sidhu and Kanho Murmu:**
 
 
• They were the key leaders of the Santhal Rebellion, who mobilized thousands of tribal people in the fight against colonial oppression.
 
• Their leadership remains a symbol of tribal resistance in Indian history.
 
 
 
• **Impact of Santhal Rebellion:**
 
 
• It highlighted the grievances of tribal communities under British rule, especially regarding land alienation and exploitation.
 
• It led to administrative changes, including the establishment of the Santhal Pargana district.

questions.question:
Which of the following statements is/are correct regarding the Indian National Congress (INC)?

a) The INC was founded in 1885 by Allan Octavian Hume.

b) The first session of the INC was held in Pune under the presidency of WC Bonnerjee.
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Only a**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• The **Indian National Congress (INC)** was founded in **December 1885 **by **Allan Octavian Hume**, a retired British civil servant.
 
• The INC aimed to provide a platform for Indians to express their political, economic, and social grievances under British rule.
 
• The** first session** of the INC was held in **December 1885 **at **Bombay** (not Pune), presided over by **Womesh Chunder Bonnerjee**.
 
• The INC played a pivotal role in India’s struggle for independence, evolving from moderate demands to advocating for complete self-rule.
 
• The INC's establishment marked the beginning of organized political activity in India, laying the foundation for future mass movements.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Allan Octavian Hume**: Known as the "Father of the Indian National Congress," Hume envisioned the INC as a safety valve for discontent among Indians.
 
• **Womesh Chunder Bonnerjee**: A prominent lawyer and the first president of the INC, Bonnerjee emphasized the importance of gradual reforms and cooperation with the British government.
 
• **Initial Objectives of INC**: The INC initially focused on moderate demands such as reforms in British administration, reduction in military expenditure, and increased representation of Indians in government services.
 
• **Moderates vs. Extremists**: By the early 20th century, the INC saw ideological divisions between Moderates, who advocated constitutional reforms, and Extremists, who sought more assertive measures, including self-rule.
 
• **Role in Freedom Struggle**: Post-1915, under leaders like Mahatma Gandhi, the INC transitioned into a mass movement advocating nonviolent resistance and played a crucial role in India’s independence in 1947.

questions.question: Bhawani Pathak and Devi Choudhurani were famous leaders associated with which of the following?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Fakir and Sanyasi Rebellion**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• **Bhawani Pathak and Devi Choudhurani** were prominent leaders of the **Fakir and Sanyasi Rebellion**, which took place in Bengal during the late 18th century.
 
• The rebellion was primarily a reaction against the oppressive policies of the British East India Company, including high land revenue demands and exploitation.
 
• The Fakir and Sanyasi Rebellion was led by ascetic groups, including Fakirs (Muslim ascetics) and Sanyasis (Hindu ascetics), who united to resist British colonial rule.
 
• The rebellion gained widespread support from the local population, particularly peasants who were suffering under British economic policies.
 
• The movement is remembered for its unique blend of religious unity and social justice, symbolized by leaders like Bhawani Pathak and Devi Choudhurani.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Fakir and Sanyasi Rebellion**

 
 
• This rebellion occurred in Bengal between the late 18th and early 19th centuries and is considered one of the earliest signs of resistance against British colonialism.
 
• The uprising was triggered by the devastating famine of 1770 and the exploitative revenue policies of the British East India Company.
 
• The rebellion involved guerrilla warfare tactics, with ascetics and local peasants attacking British officials and establishments.
 
• Although ultimately suppressed, the rebellion highlighted the growing discontent among Indians against colonial rule.
 
 
 
• **Bhawani Pathak**
 
 
• Bhawani Pathak was a legendary leader and fighter associated with the Fakir and Sanyasi Rebellion.
 
• He is often depicted as a Robin Hood-like figure who fought against British exploitation and assisted the oppressed peasants.
 
• His leadership inspired many to join the resistance movement.
 
 
 
• **Devi Choudhurani**
 
 
• Devi Choudhurani was another iconic leader of the rebellion, known for her bravery and strategic acumen.
 
• She is celebrated as a female revolutionary in Indian history, often referenced in literature and folklore.
 
• Her story was popularized by Bankim Chandra Chattopadhyay in his novel "Devi Chaudhurani."
 
 
 
• **Social and Economic Impact**
 
 
• The rebellion underscored the grievances of Indian peasants against British economic policies.
 
• It paved the way for future uprisings and contributed to the early nationalist sentiment in India.
 
• The movement also emphasized the role of religious unity in resisting colonial oppression.

questions.question: Who authored the book 'Hind Swaraj', which outlined the principles of non-violent resistance and self-rule?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Mahatma Gandhi**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• **'Hind Swaraj'** was written by Mahatma Gandhi in **1909** during his voyage from **England to South Africa**.
 
• The book outlines Gandhi's **philosophy of non-violent resistance** (Satyagraha) and his vision of self-rule (Swaraj) for India.
 
• It critiques Western civilization and industrialization, advocating for a return to **simple, self-sufficient village life**.
 
• The book serves as a foundational text for the Indian independence movement and reflects Gandhi's belief in **truth, non-violence, and self-reliance**.
 
• 'Hind Swaraj' has been translated into several languages and remains a key text in understanding **Gandhian philosophy**.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Satyagraha:**

 
 
• A key concept in Gandhi's philosophy, it means **"insistence on truth"** or non-violent resistance.
 
• It was employed in various movements such as the **Champaran Satyagraha** and the **Dandi March**.
 
• Satyagraha emphasizes moral strength over physical force to achieve justice and freedom.
 
 
 
• **Swaraj:**
 
 
• Literally translates to **"self-rule"** or "**self-governance**."
 
• In 'Hind Swaraj,' Gandhi advocated for Swaraj not just as political independence but also as **individual and community self-reliance**.
 
• It involves decentralization of power and promotion of local industries and sustainability.
 
 
 
• **Critique of Western Civilization:**
 
 
• In 'Hind Swaraj,' Gandhi criticizes the materialism and industrialization of Western societies.
 
• He attributes the erosion of moral and spiritual values to the **overemphasis on machinery and technology**.
 
• Instead, he advocates for a lifestyle rooted in simplicity, spirituality, and community well-being.

questions.question: Who among the following is NOT considered a leader of the Moderates in the Indian National Congress?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Aurobindo Ghosh**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• Aurobindo Ghosh is primarily associated with the **Extremist faction** of the Indian National Congress, not the Moderates.
 
• He played a significant role in promoting **radical nationalism** and advocating for complete independence rather than gradual reforms.
 
• During the early 1900s, Aurobindo Ghosh emerged as a key leader of the Extremists alongside Bal Gangadhar Tilak and Bipin Chandra Pal.
 
• His political philosophy included the use of **passive resistance** and boycotts to oppose British rule.
 
• He later retired from active politics and shifted his focus to spirituality, establishing the **Sri Aurobindo Ashram** in Puducherry.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Moderates in the Indian National Congress**

 
 
• Moderates were a group of leaders in the Congress who believed in achieving political reforms through **constitutional and peaceful methods.**
 
• Key leaders included **Dadabhai Naoroji, Gopal Krishna Gokhale and Ferozshah Mehta.**
 
• Their primary aim was to secure **greater representation for Indians in the legislative councils** and administrative reforms.
 
• They often relied on **petitions, speeches, and lobbying** to achieve their goals.
 
 
 
• **Extremists in the Indian National Congress**
 
 
• Extremists were a faction within the Congress that emerged in the early 1900s, advocating for **direct action and complete independence.**
 
• Key leaders included **Bal Gangadhar Tilak, Bipin Chandra Pal, and Lala Lajpat Rai.**
 
• They used methods like **boycotts, Swadeshi movement, and mass mobilization** to challenge British rule.
 
• The split between Moderates and Extremists occurred at the **Surat Session of the Congress in 1907.**
 
 
 
• **Dadabhai Naoroji**
 
 
• Known as the "Grand Old Man of India," Dadabhai Naoroji was a prominent Moderate leader.
 
• He authored the book **"Poverty and Un-British Rule in India,"** highlighting the economic drain caused by British policies.
 
• He was the first Indian to be elected to the British Parliament in 1892.
 
 
 
• **Gopal Krishna Gokhale**
 
 
• A Moderate leader and mentor to Mahatma Gandhi, Gokhale was a staunch advocate of **social reforms and education.**
 
• He founded the **Servants of India Society** to promote social welfare and national awakening.

questions.question: What was the main reason for the protest against the Simon Commission in 1928?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Lack of Indian representation**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• The Simon Commission, formed in 1927, was an all-European body with no Indian members, which led to widespread resentment among Indians.
 
• It was tasked with reviewing the working of the Government of India Act, 1919, but Indians felt excluded from decisions about their own governance.
 
• Protests against the Commission began when it arrived in India in 1928, with slogans like "Simon Go Back" echoing across the country.
 
• Major leaders, including the Indian National Congress, boycotted the Commission, viewing it as a symbol of colonial arrogance and disregard for Indian aspirations.
 
• The lack of Indian representation in the Simon Commission highlighted the demand for greater self-governance and autonomy, fueling the freedom struggle further.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Simon Commission**

 
 
• It was officially known as the Indian Statutory Commission, formed under the chairmanship of Sir John Simon.
 
• The Commission was set up to evaluate the constitutional reforms introduced by the Government of India Act, 1919.
 
• The absence of Indian members in the Commission was seen as a deliberate exclusion, sparking national outrage.
 
 
 
• **Lala Lajpat Rai's Protest**
 
 
• During a protest in Lahore against the Simon Commission, Lala Lajpat Rai was brutally lathi-charged by the police.
 
• He succumbed to his injuries later, becoming a martyr for the Indian independence movement.
 
 
 
• **Government of India Act, 1919**
 
 
• This Act introduced dyarchy (dual governance) in the provinces, dividing subjects into "Reserved" and "Transferred" categories.
 
• The dissatisfaction with its limited scope of reforms eventually led to demands for more substantive constitutional changes.
 
 
 
• **Impact of the Protests**
 
 
• The protests against the Simon Commission marked a significant moment in India's fight for self-rule.
 
• It united Indians across political and social lines, strengthening the push for complete independence.

questions.question: Which leader presided over the 1929 Lahore Session of the Indian National Congress, where the resolution for 'Purna Swaraj' was passed?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Jawaharlal Nehru**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• The **Lahore Session of the Indian National Congress** was held in December 1929 and presided over by **Jawaharlal Nehru**.
 
• During this session, the Congress passed the historic resolution for **'Purna Swaraj' (Complete Independence)**, declaring India's goal to achieve total freedom from British rule.
 
• January 26, 1930, was declared as **Independence Day**, where Indians were to pledge for complete independence.
 
• The resolution also marked the adoption of the **tricolor flag** as the national flag, symbolizing unity and the spirit of freedom.
 
• This session was a turning point in the Indian freedom struggle, shifting focus from dominion status to complete independence.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Jawaharlal Nehru**

 
 
• He was one of the central figures in the Indian freedom struggle and became the first Prime Minister of independent India in 1947.
 
• Known for his vision of a modern, secular, and democratic India.
 
• Authored the famous book *'The Discovery of India'*, reflecting on India's history, culture, and philosophy.
 
 
 
• **Purna Swaraj Declaration**
 
 
• It was adopted to demand complete independence from British rule, replacing the earlier demand for dominion status.
 
• The declaration highlighted the exploitation of India under colonial rule and called for self-governance.
 
 
 
• **Lahore Session of 1929**
 
 
• It was held on the banks of the Ravi River in Lahore (now in Pakistan).
 
• It marked a decisive shift in the Indian National Congress's approach towards the freedom movement.
 
 
 
• **January 26 as a Historical Date**
 
 
• January 26, 1930, was observed as the first Independence Day across India.
 
• This date was later chosen for the adoption of the Indian Constitution in 1950, marking the Republic Day of India.

questions.question: The Swadeshi Movement, launched to oppose the partition of Bengal and promote Indian goods, began in which year?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**1905**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• The Swadeshi Movement was launched in **1905** as a protest against the partition of Bengal by Lord Curzon.
 
• It advocated the use of **Indian-made goods** and the boycott of British products.
 
• The movement was officially started on **7 August 1905**, with a meeting at the Town Hall in Calcutta.
 
• Prominent leaders of the movement included **Bal Gangadhar Tilak, Bipin Chandra Pal, Lala Lajpat Rai, and Aurobindo Ghosh**.
 
• The Swadeshi Movement played a significant role in fostering Indian nationalism and creating awareness about self-reliance and economic independence.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Partition of Bengal**

 
 
• In **1905**, Lord Curzon divided Bengal into East Bengal and West Bengal, citing administrative convenience.
 
• The partition was perceived as an attempt to weaken the nationalist movement by dividing Hindus and Muslims.
 
• It led to widespread protests and became the catalyst for the Swadeshi Movement.
 
 
 
• **Swadeshi Ideology**
 
 
• The term "Swadeshi" means **‘of one’s own country’**.
 
• It emphasized the use of indigenous goods and services to reduce dependence on foreign products.
 
• This ideology became a cornerstone of the Indian freedom struggle.
 
 
 
• **Significance of Boycott**
 
 
• The boycott of British goods, especially textiles, was a major strategy to hurt the British economy.
 
• It led to the revival of Indian industries and handicrafts.
 
• Indian-made products like khadi gained popularity during this period.
 
 
 
• **Impact of the Movement**
 
 
• The Swadeshi Movement marked the beginning of a stronger and more organized nationalist struggle.
 
• It inspired future movements like the Non-Cooperation Movement and Civil Disobedience Movement.
 
• It also influenced cultural aspects, including literature, music, and art, promoting Indian identity.

questions.question: Which movement or idea is associated with the Wardha Scheme of Basic Education proposed in 1937?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Nai Talim or Basic Education**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• The Wardha Scheme of Basic Education, also known as **Nai Talim**, was proposed in 1937 by Mahatma Gandhi to promote education based on Indian culture and self-reliance.
 
• The scheme emphasized **learning through productive manual work**, such as spinning, weaving, and agriculture, to connect education with the practical needs of life.
 
• The medium of instruction was to be the **mother tongue**, making education accessible to the masses and reducing dependency on foreign languages like English.
 
• Nai Talim sought to eliminate the divide between manual labor and intellectual work, fostering dignity of labor and self-sufficiency.
 
• The idea was formally adopted at the **Wardha Conference (1937)**, chaired by Mahatma Gandhi, and subsequently served as a framework for basic education in India.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Meaning of Nai Talim:** Nai Talim translates to "New Education" and is based on the principle of learning by doing, integrating academic knowledge with physical labor and practical skills.
 
• **Role of Mahatma Gandhi:** Gandhi advocated for an education system that aligned with Indian traditions, values, and the rural lifestyle, focusing on self-reliance and moral development.
 
• **Key Features:** The Wardha Scheme recommended free and compulsory education for children aged 7-14, with a curriculum centered on craft-based learning and character-building.
 
• **Impact on Modern Education:** The principles of Nai Talim influenced post-independence educational reforms, emphasizing vocational training and skill development in India's education policy.
 
• **Criticism:** While idealistic, the scheme faced challenges in implementation due to a lack of trained teachers, resources, and alignment with contemporary needs.

questions.question: In which year was the Partition of Bengal, initially implemented by the British in 1905, officially annulled?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**1911**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• The Partition of Bengal was implemented by the British in 1905 under Lord Curzon’s administration, dividing Bengal into East Bengal and Assam, and West Bengal.
 
• It faced fierce opposition from Indian leaders and the general public, leading to protests, boycotts, and the Swadeshi Movement.
 
• Due to the intense backlash, the British annulled the partition in **1911** during the Delhi Durbar held to commemorate King George V's coronation.
 
• Post-annulment, Bengal was reunited, but Bihar and Orissa were carved out as separate provinces to ease administrative challenges.
 
• The annulment symbolized the growing strength of Indian nationalism and the organized resistance against British policies.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Partition of Bengal (1905):**

 
 
• The division was justified by the British as an administrative necessity due to Bengal’s large size and population.
 
• East Bengal was predominantly Muslim, while West Bengal had a Hindu majority, leading to communal undertones in the partition.
 
 
 
• **Swadeshi Movement:**
 
 
• A key response to the partition, promoting the boycott of British goods and the use of indigenous products.
 
• It marked the beginning of organized nationalist movements in India.
 
 
 
• **Delhi Durbar (1911):**
 
 
• It was a grand event to mark the coronation of King George V and Queen Mary.
 
• During this event, the British announced the annulment of the Partition of Bengal and the transfer of the capital from Calcutta to Delhi.
 
 
 
• **Impact on Indian Nationalism:**
 
 
• The partition and its annulment highlighted the importance of mass movements and unity among Indians.
 
• It strengthened the resolve of Indian leaders to fight for independence and helped unite various communities.

questions.question: In which year did the Bhil rebellion start under the leadership of Bhil leaders such as Kazi Singh and Bhima Naik?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**1818**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• The Bhil rebellion, led by prominent leaders such as Kazi Singh and Bhima Naik, started in **1818**.
 
• This tribal uprising occurred in the regions of **Khandesh**, which is now part of modern-day Maharashtra and Madhya Pradesh.
 
• The Bhils revolted against British colonial rule due to **exploitation, loss of autonomy, and oppressive revenue policies**.
 
• The rebellion was fueled by the marginalization of the Bhil community and the British seizure of their traditional lands and forests.
 
• Despite being tribal guerrilla fighters, the Bhils faced significant challenges in sustaining the rebellion against the superior British forces.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Bhil Community:**

 
 
• The Bhils are one of the largest tribal communities in India, primarily inhabiting the western and central parts of the country.
 
• Traditionally, they relied on agriculture, hunting, and forest resources for sustenance.
 
• Their distinct cultural identity includes traditional attire, unique art forms, and tribal governance systems.
 
 
 
• **Causes of Tribal Rebellions:**
 
 
• The British colonial policies often disrupted tribal autonomy and traditional ways of life.
 
• Exploitation by landlords, moneylenders, and revenue officials further aggravated tribal discontent.
 
• Forced labor and displacement from ancestral lands were recurring issues for tribal communities.
 
 
 
• **Impact of the Bhil Rebellion:**
 
 
• Although the rebellion was eventually suppressed, it highlighted the resilience and resistance of the Bhil community.
 
• The British implemented certain conciliatory measures, such as appointing Bhil leaders in administrative roles, to pacify the community.
 
 
 
• **Other Tribal Movements:**
 
 
• The Bhil rebellion was one of many tribal uprisings during British rule, such as the **Santhal rebellion (1855-1856)** and the **Munda rebellion (1899-1900)**.
 
• These movements were significant in shaping India's freedom struggle by exposing the exploitative colonial practices.

questions.question: The Poligars rebelled against the British in which Presidency, when the British tried to snatch away their military and land rights?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Madras Presidency**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• The Poligar Rebellion occurred in the **Madras Presidency** during the late 18th and early 19th centuries.
 
• Poligars were feudal chieftains under the Nayak and Vijayanagar rulers who controlled forts and commanded independent armies in South India.
 
• The rebellion was triggered when the British East India Company tried to **abolish the military and land rights of Poligars**.
 
• Key figures in the rebellion include **Kattabomman** and other Poligar leaders who resisted British authority.
 
• The suppression of the rebellion led to the consolidation of British power in South India and the dismantling of feudal structures in the region.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Poligars:**

 
 
• Poligars were local chieftains who collected taxes and maintained law and order in their respective territories.
 
• They were known for their military prowess and control over fortified regions.
 
 
 
• **Madras Presidency:**
 
 
• The Madras Presidency was a major administrative division of British India, covering most of South India.
 
• It was a hub for rebellions like the Poligar Revolt due to strong regional resistance against British policies.
 
 
 
• **Kattabomman:**
 
 
• Kattabomman was a prominent Poligar leader from Tamil Nadu who opposed British control.
 
• He became a symbol of resistance and is remembered for his courage and defiance against colonial rule.
 
 
 
• **Impact of the Rebellion:**
 
 
• The suppression of Poligars marked the decline of feudal autonomy in South India.
 
• The rebellion highlighted the growing discontent against British policies and led to stricter administrative measures.

questions.question: The first armed tribal rebellion against the British is considered to have taken place in:
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**1784**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• The** first armed tribal rebellion** against British rule in India is considered to be the **Tamar Rebellion of 1784**.
 
• This rebellion was led by the **Tamar tribe** in the Chotanagpur region (present-day Jharkhand).
 
• The Tamar tribes revolted against the exploitative policies of the British, especially related to land revenue and forced labor.
 
• It marked the beginning of resistance movements by tribal communities, which continued with uprisings like the Kol Rebellion (1831) and the Santhal Rebellion (1855).
 
• Tribal resistance was fueled by the disruption of traditional lifestyles, exploitation by landlords, and the introduction of new laws and systems by the British administration.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Tamar Rebellion:**

 
 
• It was one of the earliest tribal revolts in India, occurring in 1784.
 
• The rebellion was triggered by the British policies of heavy taxation and forced labor (begar).
 
• The leaders of the rebellion used traditional tribal warfare tactics against the British forces.
 
 
 
• **Kol Rebellion (1831-1832):**
 
 
• Led by the Kol tribes in the Chotanagpur region.
 
• It was an uprising against the British and moneylenders who exploited tribal land and resources.
 
 
 
• **Santhal Rebellion (1855-1856):**
 
 
• Also known as the Santhal Hul, this revolt was led by Sidhu and Kanhu Murmu.
 
• The Santhals revolted against the oppressive policies of the British and the zamindars.
 
 
 
• **Impact of Tribal Revolts:**
 
 
• These uprisings highlighted the plight of tribal communities under British rule.
 
• They are significant for understanding the early resistance movements in India.

questions.question: The Chuar Rebellion, which emerged as a culmination of the economic grievances of ordinary peasants and hereditary workers, reached its peak during which of the following years?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**1798-99**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• The** Chuar Rebellion** was a series of uprisings by the tribal communities, primarily the **Chuar and Bhumij tribes**, in Bengal and Bihar against British colonial rule.
 
• The rebellion occurred due to severe **economic grievances**, including the imposition of heavy land revenue and exploitation by British officials.
 
• The peak of the Chuar rebellion was witnessed during the years **1798-99**, when widespread unrest impacted regions such as **Midnapore and Jungle Mahal.**
 
• British policies, such as the Permanent Settlement Act of 1793, further alienated the tribal population by depriving them of their traditional rights to land and forest resources.
 
• The rebellion was ultimately suppressed through military interventions and administrative measures by the British.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Permanent Settlement Act (1793):**

 
 
• Implemented by Lord Cornwallis, this act introduced the zamindari system of land revenue collection.
 
• It fixed the revenue payable by zamindars permanently, depriving the tribal communities of their customary land rights.
 
 
 
• **Jungle Mahal:**
 
 
• A region in Bengal that included parts of present-day West Bengal, Odisha, and Jharkhand.
 
• The area was historically inhabited by tribal communities such as the Bhumij and Chuar.
 
 
 
• **Tribal Uprisings:**
 
 
• In the 18th and 19th centuries, several tribal rebellions occurred due to British exploitation, including the **Santhal Rebellion (1855-56)** and the **Kol Rebellion (1831-32).**
 
• These uprisings highlighted the socio-economic struggles faced by tribal populations under colonial rule.
 
 
 
• **Colonial Economic Policies:**
 
 
• British colonial policies disrupted the traditional tribal economy, leading to widespread poverty and dispossession.
 
• Heavy land taxes and restrictions on forest use exacerbated the grievances of tribal communities.

questions.question: The first parallel government, following the Quit India Movement, was established in which city?

• The Prati Sarkar was established in **1943** and lasted until **1946**.
 
• The movement was led by **Y.B. Chavan**, **Nana Patil**, and others who organized local governance systems to resist British authority.
 
• It aimed to provide an **alternate governance model** in areas liberated from British control.
 
• Satara became a center for revolutionary activities, with leaders organizing local administration, justice systems, and economic policies.
 
• The Quit India Movement, launched in **1942**, had widespread impact, but Satara's Prati Sarkar stood out as a unique example of localized governance.
 
• The Prati Sarkar also focused on **social reforms**, such as providing education and addressing grievances of the common people.
 
• This initiative showcased the **strength of grassroots-level movements** in India's struggle for independence.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 __

questions.question: Who is most commonly associated with the 'safety valve' theory regarding the formation of the Indian National Congress?
questions.solution:
The Correct answer is __**AO Hume**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• The **'Safety Valve Theory'** is associated with **AO Hume**, a retired British civil servant who played a key role in the formation of the **Indian National Congress (INC)** in 1885.
 
• This theory suggests that the British government supported the establishment of the INC as a means to provide a platform for Indians to express their grievances peacefully, thus preventing revolutionary activities.
 
• **AO Hume** believed that by channeling Indian discontent into constitutional and non-violent methods, the British could maintain control over India while addressing some concerns.
 
• He was instrumental in bringing together prominent Indian leaders and intellectuals to form the INC, which later became a significant force in India's struggle for independence.
 
• The INC was initially meant to serve as a forum for educated Indians to discuss political issues and advise the British administration on reforms.
 
• The theory has been debated by historians, with some accepting its validity and others arguing that the INC was formed due to genuine political aspirations of Indian leaders rather than British motives.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Lord Dufferin**__

 __
 
• **Lord Dufferin** was the **Viceroy of India** from 1884 to 1888.
 
• Although he did not directly form the INC, he interacted with its leaders and played a role in facilitating its early discussions.
 
• He supported the idea of addressing Indian grievances, but his involvement was more indirect compared to AO Hume.
 
 
 
• **WC Bannerji**__
 __
 
• **WC Bannerji** was the first president of the **Indian National Congress** in 1885.
 
• He was a prominent lawyer and political leader known for his advocacy of constitutional reforms and moderate politics.
 
• While he played an important role in the INC's early leadership, the 'Safety Valve Theory' is not directly associated with him.
 
 
 
• **Dadabhai Naoroji**__
 
 
• **Dadabhai Naoroji** was a key figure in Indian nationalism and the INC, often referred to as the **Grand Old Man of India**.
 
• He was known for his economic critique of British colonial rule, especially the **'Drain of Wealth' theory.**
 
• Though he contributed significantly to the INC, his focus was more on economic issues rather than the 'Safety Valve Theory.'

questions.question: The book "Gita Rahasya", a philosophical interpretation of the Bhagavad Gita, was written by which of the following leaders?

__
 
• **Gita Rahasya**, also known as **Srimad Bhagavad Gita Rahasya**, is a famous philosophical interpretation of the **Bhagavad Gita**.
 
• It was written by **Bal Gangadhar Tilak**, a prominent freedom fighter, social reformer, and nationalist leader during the Indian independence movement.
 
• Tilak wrote this book while he was imprisoned in the **Mandalay jail** (Burma) during the years **1908-1914**.
 
• In the book, Tilak emphasizes the concept of **Karma Yoga**, which highlights the importance of performing one's duty selflessly without attachment to the results.
 
• Tilak believed that the Bhagavad Gita was not merely a religious text but a guide for active participation in life and society.
 
• He used the teachings of the Gita to inspire Indians to fight for their rights and freedom during the colonial period.
 
• The book is written in **Marathi** and has been translated into various other languages over time.
 
• Tilak was often referred to as the "**Lion of Maharashtra**" for his bold stance against British rule and his advocacy for Swaraj (self-rule).

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

• **Gopal Krishna Gokhale**__

 __
 
• Gopal Krishna Gokhale was a renowned **social reformer and moderate leader** in the Indian National Congress.
 
• He was the founder of the **Servants of India Society**, which aimed to promote education and social welfare.
 
• Gokhale was a mentor to **Mahatma Gandhi** and played a key role in shaping Gandhi's early political views.
 
• Despite his contributions to India's freedom struggle, he did not write Gita Rahasya.
 
 
 
• **Mahatma Gandhi**__
 __
 
• Mahatma Gandhi is known as the "**Father of the Nation**" in India for his pivotal role in the freedom struggle.
 
• Gandhi's philosophy was centered around **non-violence (Ahimsa)** and **truth (Satya)**.
 
• He authored several books, including **Hind Swaraj**, but he did not write Gita Rahasya.
 
 
 
• **Aurobindo Ghosh**__
 
 
• Aurobindo Ghosh was a revolutionary turned spiritual leader who founded the **Aurobindo Ashram** in Pondicherry.
 
• His writings on the Bhagavad Gita focus on its spiritual and metaphysical aspects, particularly in his work **Essays on the Gita**.
 
• However, he was not the author of Gita Rahasya.

questions.question: VO Chidambaram Pillai was actively involved in the revolutionary movement in which of the following areas?

questions.question: In 1892, the Indian National Congress passed a significant resolution at its Allahabad Session, which was a demand for the inclusion of Indians in which of the following?
questions.solution:

__
 
• In 1892, during the Allahabad Session of the Indian National Congress, a resolution was passed demanding **increased representation of Indians in the Legislative Council**.
 
• The resolution was part of the early phase of the Congress, which focused on **constitutional reforms and political representation**.
 
• The demands aimed at ensuring that Indians had a voice in the governance of the country under British rule.
 
• This resolution marked a significant step in the gradual evolution of the Indian National Congress's political objectives.
 
• Such demands eventually laid the groundwork for **subsequent reforms like the Indian Councils Act of 1892**, which allowed limited Indian participation in the legislative process.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Indian Councils Act of 1892**

 
 
• The Indian Councils Act of 1892 was an important legislative reform introduced by the British government.
 
• It expanded the powers of Legislative Councils, allowing members to **ask questions on the budget and other public matters**.
 
• While the Act was limited in scope, it was a small step toward involving Indians in governance.
 
 
 
• **Indian National Congress (INC)**
 
 
• The INC was founded in 1885 by Allan Octavian Hume, Dadabhai Naoroji, and Dinshaw Wacha.
 
• In its early years, the Congress focused on **moderate demands**, such as representation in councils and administrative reforms.
 
 
 
• **Allahabad Session of 1892**
 
 
• This session reflected the growing **demand for political rights** among Indians.
 
• It highlighted the role of the Congress in articulating constitutional demands during the pre-Gandhian era.
 
 
 
• **Viceroy’s Legislative Council**
 
 
• Under British rule, the Viceroy's Legislative Council was the primary legislative body.
 
• Indians were initially excluded but were gradually allowed limited participation following persistent demands.

questions.question: Roots of which of the following revolts lied in the fact that the British deprived the tribals of their traditional rights over the toddy trees?

• The immediate trigger for the revolt was the **deprivation of traditional rights over toddy trees**, which were a crucial livelihood resource for the Koya tribes.
 
• British policies, including **imposition of taxes** and restrictions on forest resources, deeply affected the tribal communities.
 
• The Koya tribes, along with other tribal groups, revolted to protect their **land, resources, and cultural autonomy**.

• **Toddy Trees:**

 
 
• Toddy trees, such as palm and date trees, were a key source of livelihood for tribal communities.
 
• They were used for producing toddy, a traditional fermented drink, and were also economically significant.
 
• British policies restricting access to these trees disrupted the tribal economy.
 
 
 
• **Impact of British Colonial Policies:**
 
 
• Colonial administration introduced **land revenue systems** and forest laws that marginalized tribal communities.
 
• Tribals were forced to pay taxes and lost access to traditional resources like forests and toddy trees.
 
• These policies led to widespread dissatisfaction and revolts among tribal groups.
 
 
 
• **Tribal Resistance Movements:**
 
 
• Several tribal revolts occurred during British rule, including the **Santhal Rebellion (1855-56)** and the **Munda Rebellion (1899-1900).**
 
• These movements often aimed to protect tribal lands and resources from colonial exploitation.
 
 
 
• **Legacy of Tribal Revolts:**

• The movement aimed at advocating for the **purification of Islam**, strict adherence to Islamic law, and the eradication of un-Islamic practices.
 
• It primarily focused on **religious and social reforms** rather than a direct challenge to colonial rule, thus distinguishing it from tribal revolts.
 
• The movement gained traction among the **rural Muslim peasants**, addressing issues like exploitation by landlords and British indigo planters.
 
• The Farazis resisted the oppression of the zamindars, but their resistance was largely **non-violent** and religious in nature.
 
• Its main objective was to restore the **purity of Islam** and to create an ideal Islamic society.
 
• Unlike tribal revolts, the Farazi Movement was not led by tribal communities or aimed at preserving tribal autonomy or culture.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Kherwar Movement**__

 __
 
• The **Kherwar Movement** was a tribal uprising led by the **Santhal community** in the late 19th century.
 
• This movement was initiated under the leadership of **Bhagirath Majhi** and aimed at establishing **Santhal self-rule** and reclaiming their traditional rights over land.
 
• It was deeply rooted in the socio-religious beliefs of the Santhals and sought to challenge the dominance of zamindars and British officials.
 
• The movement had elements of both socio-religious reform and political resistance, making it a tribal revolt.
 
 
 
• **Tamar Revolts**__
 __
 
• The **Tamar Revolts** were a series of uprisings by the **Munda tribe** in the Tamar region of present-day **Jharkhand**.
 
• The revolts were led by tribal leaders like **Birsa Munda** and were aimed at resisting the exploitation and oppression of the Mundas by landlords (dikus) and British officials.
 
• It was a classic example of a tribal revolt, focusing on the restoration of tribal autonomy and rights over forest and agricultural lands.
 
 
 
• **Santhal Revolt**__
 
 
• The **Santhal Revolt** (1855–1856) was a major tribal uprising led by the **Santhal community** in present-day Jharkhand and West Bengal.
 
• This rebellion was led by the **Murmu brothers** (Sidhu and Kanhu) and was directed against the exploitation by **zamindars, moneylenders, and the British administration.**
 
• The Santhals sought to establish a **self-governed state** free from external interference and oppression.
 
• The revolt was characterized by its intensity and the mobilization of a large number of tribal people.

questions.question: Which leader collaborated with Mahatma Gandhi during the Kheda Satyagraha in 1918?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Sardar Vallabhbhai Patel**__.

__
 
• Sardar Vallabhbhai Patel was one of the key leaders who collaborated with Mahatma Gandhi during the **Kheda Satyagraha of 1918**.
 
• The Kheda Satyagraha was organized against the **British government's decision to levy taxes despite crop failure and famine conditions in Gujarat**.
 
• Sardar Patel played a pivotal role in mobilizing peasants and organizing them for the non-violent protest under Gandhi's leadership.
 
• The movement achieved success as the British government agreed to suspend tax collection for the affected areas and provide relief to the farmers.
 
• The Kheda Satyagraha marked one of the first major movements led by Gandhi in India, with strong support from Sardar Patel and other leaders.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Kheda Satyagraha:**

 
 
• It was a non-violent civil disobedience movement led by Mahatma Gandhi in Gujarat.
 
• The movement focused on addressing the unjust tax policies imposed on farmers during a period of severe drought and famine.
 
• It involved mass participation of farmers, emphasizing the principles of Satyagraha (truth and non-violence).
 
 
 
• **Sardar Vallabhbhai Patel:**
 
 
• Popularly known as the "Iron Man of India," Patel is celebrated for his leadership and dedication to India's independence and unity.
 
• He played a significant role in organizing farmers and leading several agrarian movements, including the Kheda and Bardoli Satyagrahas.
 
• Patel later became India's first Deputy Prime Minister and Home Minister, contributing to the integration of princely states into the Indian Union.
 
 
 
• **Connection to Gandhi:**
 
 
• Sardar Patel was deeply influenced by Mahatma Gandhi's philosophy of non-violence and truth.
 
• He worked closely with Gandhi in various movements, including the Kheda Satyagraha and the Salt March.
 
 
 
• **Impact of Kheda Satyagraha:**
 
 
• It highlighted the plight of peasants under colonial rule and demonstrated the effectiveness of organized, non-violent resistance.
 
• The success of the movement boosted Gandhi's leadership stature and introduced Sardar Patel as a prominent national leader.

questions.question: Who was the leader of the 'Indian National Army' before Subhas Chandra Bose took charge?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Mohan Singh**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• **Mohan Singh** was an Indian military officer and a key figure in the formation of the **Indian National Army (INA)**.
 
• The INA was initially formed in 1942 in Singapore with the help of the Japanese Army, and Mohan Singh became its first leader.
 
• He envisioned the INA as a force to liberate India from British colonial rule by allying with Japan during World War II.
 
• However, due to differences with the Japanese leadership over the treatment of INA soldiers and strategic decisions, Mohan Singh disbanded the INA in late 1942.
 
• When Subhas Chandra Bose assumed leadership of the INA in 1943, he reorganized and revitalized the movement, giving it a new direction and purpose.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Indian National Army (INA):** The INA was formed to fight against British colonial rule and was composed mainly of Indian soldiers captured by the Japanese during World War II.
 
• **Subhas Chandra Bose:** Bose took over as the leader of the INA in 1943 and renamed it the "Azad Hind Fauj." Under his leadership, the INA adopted the slogan "Jai Hind."
 
• **Singapore Conference 1942:** The INA was first established at the Indian Independence League conference in Singapore, with Mohan Singh as its commander-in-chief.
 
• **Arzi Hukumat-e-Azad Hind:** Subhas Chandra Bose also established a provisional government of Free India (Azad Hind Government) in 1943 to support the INA's efforts.
 
• **Japan's Role:** Japan provided logistical and military support to the INA, as they sought to weaken British colonial power in Asia during World War II.

questions.question: What is the title of the poetry collection by Michael Madhusudan Dutt, published in 1849, that narrates the story of Prithviraj Chauhan?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**The Captive Lady**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• **The Captive Lady** is a narrative poem written by Michael Madhusudan Dutt, published in the year **1849**.
 
• The poem is based on the story of **Prithviraj Chauhan**, the legendary Rajput king of Ajmer and Delhi.
 
• Michael Madhusudan Dutt, an iconic figure in Bengali literature, wrote this work during his early career when he was experimenting with English literary traditions.
 
• The poetry reflects Dutt's fascination with historical themes and his ability to incorporate romantic and heroic elements into his works.
 
• "The Captive Lady" is one of the significant examples of his attempt to blend Indian historical narratives with Western poetic forms.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Michael Madhusudan Dutt**: Known as the pioneer of Bengali blank verse, Dutt was one of the earliest Indian poets to compose extensively in English and Bengali.
 
• **Prithviraj Chauhan**: A legendary Rajput ruler, his story is remembered for his valor and tragic romance with Princess Sanyogita.
 
• **Narrative Poetry**: A form of poetry that tells a story, often involving characters and a plot, which is central to works like "The Captive Lady."
 
• **Colonial Influence**: During the 19th century, Indian writers like Dutt were greatly influenced by Western literary traditions, leading to a fusion of Indian themes with English poetic forms.
 
• **Historical Context**: "The Captive Lady" reflects Dutt's engagement with India's rich history and culture during a time when nationalism and identity were emerging themes in literature.

questions.question: Who among the following spearheaded an active non-cooperation movement famously known as the ‘Barasat Rebellion’ against the British indigo planters?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Titu Mir**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• **Titu Mir** was a Bengali freedom fighter who led the 'Barasat Rebellion' against oppressive British indigo planters in Bengal.
 
• Born as Syed Mir Nisar Ali in 1782, Titu Mir used Islamic principles to unite farmers and weavers against exploitation.
 
• The rebellion occurred in 1831, where Titu Mir and his followers built a stronghold, the **bamboo fort** (Banser Kella), to resist British forces.
 
• He opposed the exploitative practices of indigo cultivation, high taxes, and the zamindari system enforced by British-backed landlords.
 
• Titu Mir was martyred in the struggle, but his movement is remembered as one of the early peasant revolts against British colonial rule.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Indigo Rebellion (1859-60):** Another significant peasant uprising in Bengal against the British indigo planters, where farmers refused to grow indigo due to exploitation.
 
• **Zamindari System:** Introduced by the British under the Permanent Settlement Act of 1793, this system empowered zamindars to collect taxes, often leading to severe exploitation of peasants.
 
• **Peasant Movements in India:** Titu Mir’s rebellion was one of the earliest organized uprisings, followed by others like the Santhal Rebellion (1855-56) and the Tebhaga Movement (1946-47).
 
• **Bamboo Fort:** Titu Mir’s fort was an innovative structure made of bamboo, symbolizing indigenous resistance against modern weaponry of the British.
 
• **Legacy:** Titu Mir is regarded as a hero in the fight for social and economic justice, inspiring future movements for India's independence.

questions.question: Who headed the 1915 committee to examine the co-operative movement in India?
questions.solution:
The Correct answer is __**Sir Edward Maclagan**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Sir Edward Maclagan** was an important figure in the history of cooperative movements in India.
 
• He headed the **1915 Committee**, which was formed to examine the **cooperative movement** in India.
 
• The committee was tasked with studying the functioning and **impact of cooperative societies** and their role in the development of rural areas.
 
• The findings of the committee emphasized the importance of **cooperatives** as a tool for **economic and social upliftment** in the country.
 
• It laid the foundation for further reforms and development in the cooperative sector, including the introduction of the **Cooperative Societies Act**.
 
• The committee recommended measures to improve the **efficiency** and expand the reach of cooperative societies in India.
 
• Cooperative movements were seen as vital for addressing issues like **rural credit shortages** and promoting **self-reliance** among farmers and rural communities.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Lord Curzon**__

 __
 
• **Lord Curzon** was a British statesman who served as the **Viceroy of India** from 1899 to 1905.
 
• He is known for his controversial decision to **partition Bengal** in 1905, which led to widespread protests and the eventual reversal of the partition in 1911.
 
• He played a key role in the establishment of the **Archaeological Survey of India** to preserve historical monuments.
 
 
 
• **Lord Irwin**__
 __
 
• **Lord Irwin**, also known as **Edward Wood**, served as the Viceroy of India from 1926 to 1931.
 
• He is notable for signing the **Gandhi-Irwin Pact** in 1931, which marked a crucial moment in India’s struggle for independence.
 
• His tenure was marked by the **Civil Disobedience Movement** led by Mahatma Gandhi.
 
 
 
• **Sir John Simon**__
 
 
• **Sir John Simon** was a British politician and head of the **Simon Commission**, which arrived in India in 1928.
 
• The commission was tasked with reviewing the **constitutional reforms** in India but faced widespread opposition due to the absence of Indian representation.
 
• The protests against the Simon Commission were a significant event in India’s freedom struggle, leading to the demand for **Purna Swaraj** (Complete Independence).
